opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that's really the core of what we're building. The way I see it, most of the computing paradigm we've inherited is fighting against nature. Digital computers spend an enormous amount of energy suppressing noise, forcing every transistor into a clean zero or one. But the workloads we care most about now, generative AI and probabilistic machine learning, are fundamentally about sampling from complex distributions. So we're spending all this energy to remove randomness, then spending even more to simulate it with pseudorandom number generators. It's kind of absurd when you think about it.

Thermodynamic computing flips that. Instead of fighting the noise, you harness it. You build physical systems whose natural dynamics, their fluctuations and their relaxation toward equilibrium, perform the computation for you. You encode a problem in the energy landscape of the system and let physics do the sampling.

Superconducting circuits are a really natural substrate for a first demonstration of that. You get very low dissipation, you get nonlinear elements like Josephson junctions, so you can engineer interesting energy landscapes, and you get a lot of control over the noise and the couplings. And a lot of that toolkit came out of the quantum computing world, which is where I spent years. In quantum computing, noise is the enemy and you're trying to keep things coherent. In thermodynamic computing, you're in the regime where noise is a resource. It's almost the dual problem.

So superconducting thermodynamic chips are a way to prove out the physics, to show we can build these stochastic analog processors, characterize them, and run things like sampling and certain linear algebra primitives with real advantages. But long term, I don't think the paradigm is tied to superconductors. The cryogenics are a real constraint for scaling and deployment. So part of the roadmap is taking those principles and moving them into room-temperature, CMOS-compatible hardware, using thermal noise in silicon, so you can manufacture at scale and actually put this in data centers.

Zooming out, it ties into my broader view that intelligence is a physical process. Life itself is a thermodynamic phenomenon, matter organizing to capture and dissipate free energy more efficiently. If we want to scale AI by orders of magnitude, we can't keep throwing more energy at digital hardware. We need computers that are physics-native, that compute the way nature does. Superconducting thermodynamic computers are the first step down that path.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so superconducting thermodynamic computers are really where this whole journey started for me, and in some sense where it's heading. When I was doing my PhD and then at Google on quantum computing, you spend all your time fighting noise. You're trying to cool these superconducting qubits down to millikelvin temperatures, isolate them from everything, and you're constantly treating thermal fluctuations as the enemy. And at some point the thought that kept nagging at me was: what if instead of fighting the noise, you made the noise do the computation for you?

That's really the core idea behind thermodynamic computing. Most of the algorithms we actually care about in machine learning, sampling, probabilistic inference, Bayesian methods, Monte Carlo, even a lot of the linear algebra underneath them, are at their heart about randomness and relaxation to equilibrium. And nature does that for free. A physical system coupled to a heat bath will relax to a Boltzmann distribution. So if you can engineer the energy landscape of a physical device so that its equilibrium distribution is the distribution you want to sample from, you've essentially turned physics into your sampler. You just let the system thermalize and read out the result.

Now, the superconducting side specifically is interesting because that's the hardware lineage I come from, and it has some real advantages. Josephson junctions give you these very nonlinear, very fast, very low-dissipation elements. You can build oscillators and coupled networks where the dynamics are extremely rich, and critically, you can operate in a regime where thermal fluctuations are significant relative to the energy scales of the circuit, which is exactly what you want for a stochastic computer. It's almost the inverse of quantum computing. There you want thermal energy way below your qubit energy. Here you want them comparable so the system actually explores the landscape.

At Extropic, we've approached it from a few directions. We've looked at superconducting implementations, and we've also looked at room-temperature semiconductor approaches, because from a practical standpoint, if you can get the same thermodynamic computing paradigm working in standard CMOS-compatible processes without a dilution fridge, you unlock scale and cost in a way that superconductors struggle with. But the superconducting work is sort of the purest expression of the physics. It's where you can really show that you're harnessing fluctuations as a resource rather than a bug.

The way I see it fitting into the bigger picture is this. The world is going to need orders of magnitude more compute for AI, and the current paradigm of deterministic digital logic running stochastic algorithms is incredibly wasteful. You spend enormous energy generating pseudo-random numbers and simulating noise on hardware that was designed to suppress noise. Thermodynamic computing closes that gap. It's a physics-based accelerator for the probabilistic parts of AI. Superconducting thermodynamic computers are one path to that, maybe the highest-performance path for certain workloads, and more broadly they've shaped how I think about the entire stack, from the device physics up to the algorithms. Energy-based models, for instance, map almost perfectly onto this kind of hardware, so a lot of our work has been co-designing the models and the physics together rather than treating them as separate problems.

astra-6.text:
I see them as a way to make the physics of the hardware do more of the computational work. In machine learning, we spend a lot of effort using digital computers to simulate distributions and draw samples from them. A thermodynamic computer turns that around: you engineer a physical system whose dynamics produce useful samples, and then you figure out how to program and train that system.

Superconducting circuits are an interesting platform for exploring that. But the question is whether you can turn the underlying physics into a practical advantage once you include the refrigeration, control, and readout. You have to account for the whole machine.

So I see this fitting into a broader effort to co-design learning algorithms and physical hardware. What models naturally map onto these devices? What can we train reliably? And where does letting a system fluctuate and relax give us something computationally useful? That’s the connection that interests me.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as a way of making the physics do more of the computation. In a conventional computer, we spend a lot of effort suppressing fluctuations and making everything behave deterministically. With thermodynamic computing, you’re asking whether those fluctuations and the system’s relaxation dynamics can become useful computational resources—for example, for sampling from a probability distribution.

That’s interesting for machine learning because sampling is often an expensive part of the problem. You could imagine a hybrid system where conventional hardware handles the control and learning updates, and a superconducting device provides some of those stochastic dynamics. The important question is whether that gives you a useful advantage once you account for the whole system, including refrigeration and getting information into and out of the device. That’s something you have to demonstrate, rather than assume from the physics alone.
